inline.s: Glancing here and glancing there, doubting here and doubting there, until the doubt reaches the point where thought and reflection are cut off — like a silver mountain and an iron wall, with no place to turn or to draw breath. At that very moment
of a sudden one knocks against it and touches it, and the true meaning of no-birth

, of a sudden surges forth. Then one's whole body is bathed in sweat, as if awakening from a great dream. Only at this point does one believe that birth is no-birth, that no-birth is birth; that investigation (cān) is precisely reflection (niàn), and reflection is precisely investigation. Turning back to look, one realizes that all along one has been, as within the Hanyuan Palace, seeking the city of Chang'an.

[The true meaning of no-birth] It refers to one's original nature. Master Hanshan says:
“At first one uses the mind to gaze and pursue; pursuing until the single thought is severed at both ends, the middle

is of itself alone — and still pressing straight on from this lone place with keen spirit, of a sudden the mass of doubt bursts apart, and one's original face of itself manifests: this very thing is the single thought of the true meaning of no-birth. If the student but has this single thought of no-birth appear before him, then in every place he gains great benefit, and this is the very time of escaping birth and death.”

(The Dream-Wandering Collection: Reply to Commissioner Yuan Cangru) [As if seeking Chang'an within the Hanyuan Palace] The Hanyuan Palace was the main hall of the imperial palace in Chang'an, the capital of the Tang dynasty. “As if seeking Chang'an within the Hanyuan Palace” is a metaphor for one who is originally a Buddha yet seeks to become a Buddha.

When one practices thus, the thing most to be feared is harboring a mind that wants to awaken. The moment a mind that wants to awaken arises, that itself is the plank blocking the way. Just keep on going straight ahead, without reckoning the stages of the work. When you reach the point where you can no longer go on, stir up your spirit and begin anew from the beginning. Moreover, do not on any account crave the mysterious and profound. Even if there is a single moment of stillness, of serene joy, do not regard it as something good, but let it go at once. Do not take the profound words and wonderful phrases of the Buddhas and patriarchs as evidence and treat them as the Dharma, and do not sink into the shell of having nothing to do, taking that as attainment.

[The plank blocking the way] A wooden board that blocks the line of sight — a metaphor for the mind that wants to awaken, which is precisely the obstacle that blocks the sight of the Way. [The shell of having nothing to do] The shell of a carefree time-waster — it refers to an empty sitting in stillness with neither deluded thoughts nor active investigation. Master Fayen says:

“One must stir up keen spirit, take up a huatou (topic of meditation), investigating it by day and by night, pressing on against it. One must not sit within the shell of having nothing to do, and one must not sit rigid as a corpse upon the cushion. If stray thoughts keep turning and multiplying, gently let them go, rise and walk a while, then take the cushion again. Open both eyes, clench both fists, straighten the spine, and once more take up the huatou as before. Then you will feel cool and clear, just as when a ladle of cold water is poured into a pot of boiling soup. Practicing thus, there will surely come a time when you reach home.”

pay no heed at all to sages and ordinary beings, to delusion and awakening; simply and only pursue where this single thought falls. Pursue it to the point of driving it to the last and killing it utterly, and after a long time one of itself sees one's original face, as meeting one's own father at a crossroads — no longer needing to seek him anywhere. Looked at this way, this matter is originally the concern of each person's own lot; there is nothing especially strange about it. If the seeker truly and sincerely acts for the matter of birth and death, let him set his hand here, and he will surely not be deceived.
